newsitem.title: USA: Lobbyist for Tyson Foods is indicted in Espy probe.
newsitem.headline: Lobbyist for Tyson Foods is indicted in Espy probe.

text.p: A Washington lobbyist for Tyson Foods, the nation's biggest poultry processor, was indicted Tuesday for allegedly lying to government investigators of former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy.

The indictment marks the first time in the Espy investigation that a Tyson employee has been charged with criminal conduct and it could prove embarrassing for the Clinton White House. As a former governor of Arkansas, President Clinton has long had close relations with the Arkansas-based company and its chairman, Don Tyson.
Tuesday's action could also be a precursor to an indictment of the Tyson corporation and top company officials, including Don Tyson, sources close to the investigation said.

"The investigation into the gratuity-giving conduct of Tyson Foods, including the individuals that are responsible for that in the Tyson structure, is active and ongoing," one of the sources, who did not want to be identified, said. "You can certainly not rule out an indictment against Tyson Foods and the responsible individuals."

A federal grand jury Tuesday charged Tyson Foods lobbyist Jack Williams with knowingly making false statements to the FBI and the Agriculture Department's Office of Inspector General during preliminary scrutiny of Espy in early 1994.

The alleged crime took place before Independent Counsel Donald Smaltz was named to head a special investigation. In the sprawling two-year probe of Espy, five sets of indictments have now targeted more than a dozen individuals and concerns.
Espy resigned as a Cabinet secretary in 1994 amid a swirl of accusations that he accepted illegal gifts and favours from companies his agency was in charge of regulating, including Tyson Foods.

In his dealings with Tyson, Espy may have violated the long-standing Federal Meat Inspection Act, which specifically bars anyone involved in meat inspection from accepting anything of value from the meat-processing industry.
The Agriculture Department is in charge of the nation's meat inspection system, and Espy was criticised early in his tenure for being lenient in regulating the poultry industry.

Tyson Foods, with annual sales of over $5 billion, allegedly wined and dined Espy and his girlfriend in 1993 and 1994 with gifts that included tickets and limousine transportation to Super Bowl playoffs in Dallas, as well as allegedly giving his girlfriend a scholarship potentially worth almost $10,000.

The company is also alleged to have paid for the then assistant secretary of agriculture in charge of marketing and inspection services to attend a University of Arkansas basketball game in Fayetteville, Arkansas.
It has consistently denied it ever tried to use its clout with Espy and the White House to gain special treatment and has promised to fight any indictments until the "bitter end."

Henry Schuelke, attorney for Williams, the Tyson lobbyist, said his client denied all charges and intended to fight the indictment vigorously. Schuelke said Williams would not agree to any out-of-court settlement with the government.

The investigation of Espy has resulted in indictments against Espy's brother Henry, the nation's second-largest crop insurance company and the biggest fruit cooperative in the country, Sun-Diamond Growers of California.
Sun-Diamond has been charged with plying Espy with gifts to gain influence. The Sun-Diamond trial ended in Washington on Tuesday and a verdict is expected by the end of the week.
